{{Short description|American food scientist (1926–2009)}}
'''Robert Vincent Decareau''' (May 26, 1926 – January 18, 2009)<ref name=nhnews>[http://www.nashuatelegraph.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20090120/OBITS/301209982 ''Nashua (NH) Telegraph'' 20 January 2009 article on Decareau's death.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200418080945/http://www.nashuatelegraph.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20090120/OBITS/301209982 |date=18 April 2020 }} - accessed 25 July 2009.</ref> was an American [[food science|food scientist]] who was involved in the development of [[Microwave oven|microwave]] applications in [[food technology]], specifically technology that would lead to the development of the [[microwave oven]]. He also served in the [[United States Navy]] during [[World War II]] and in the [[United States Army]] during the [[Korean War]]. Decareau also was charter member of [[Phi Tau Sigma]] while pursuing his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]].

==Early life==
Decareau was born in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]], but lived in the [[Arlington, Massachusetts|Arlington]] and [[Burlington, Massachusetts|Burlington]] areas.<ref name=nhnews /> After graduating in 1943, he enlisted in the US Navy, serving aboard the [[USS Randolph (CV-15)|USS ''Randolph'']] [[aircraft carrier]] as an [[Anti-aircraft warfare|anti-aircraft gunner]].<ref name=nhnews /> While aboard the ''Randolph'', Decareau survived two [[kamikaze]] attacks in early 1945.<ref name=nhnews />

===Return home and back to service===
After World War II, Decareau returned to Massachusetts, enrolling at the University of Massachusetts at [[Amherst, Massachusetts|Amherst]].<ref name=nhnews /> There, he earned two degrees in [[chemistry]] with his [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor's degree]] in 1949 and his [[Master's degree]] in 1951.<ref name=nhnews /> After earning his master's degree, Decareau was commissioned as a [[First Lieutenant]] in the US Army during the Korean War, though he was stationed in [[Linz, Austria]].<ref name=nhnews /> While in Austria, Decareau met his wife; he would be married to the former Rosa Kaiser until his death.<ref name=nhnews />

===Back to school and Phi Tau Sigma===
After his discharge from the US Army, Decareau returned to the University of Massachusetts Amherst to pursue his Ph.D. in chemistry.<ref name=nhnews /> Decareau also became a charter member of Phi Tau Sigma.<ref name=nhnews />

==Industrial career==
After earning his Ph.D. in 1955, Decareau worked for [[Raytheon]] in [[Allston, Massachusetts|Allston]] on microwave technology that would lead to the development of the [[microwave oven]].<ref name=boston>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090224231605/http://www.boston.com/bostonglobe/obituaries/articles/2009/01/23/robert_decareau_82_helped_develop_the_microwave_oven/ 23 January 2009 ''Boston Globe'' article on Decareau's death.] - accessed 25 July 2009.</ref> Decareau's wife, Rosa, commented that a lot of work on the microwave oven was done at their home.<ref name=boston /> Then at [[Lipton]], he was involved in [[freeze drying]].<ref name=nhnews /> In the 1960s, Decareau moved to [[Palo Alto, California]] to work with [[Litton Industries]].<ref name=nhnews /> While at Litton, he developed microwave ovens that would be the foundation of [[commerce|commercial]] versions.<ref name=nhnews /> Decareau moved back to [[Natick, Massachusetts]] later in his career to work in research and development at the [[United States Army Soldier Systems Center]] to develop [[food processing]] techniques for [[United States military|military]] and [[space exploration]] applications.<ref name=nhnews /> His work would earn him [[Fellow]]ship of the [[Institute of Food Technologists]] in 1994.<ref>[http://www.ift.org/cms/?pid=1000288 List of Fellows of the Institute of Food Technologists as of 2009.] - accessed 25 July 2009.</ref> During his career, Decareau was one of the first people to refer to himself as a food scientist.<ref>{{cite news |title=N.H. man who helped develop microwave oven dies |work=[[The Portsmouth Herald]] |date=January 20, 2009 |access-date=July 25, 2009 |url=http://www.seacoastonline.com/articles/20090120-NEWS-90120014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090122073020/http://seacoastonline.com/articles/20090120-NEWS-90120014|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 22, 2009}}</ref>

===Microwave consulting and support===
Decareau authored nine books on microwave power, including ''Microwave Processing and Engineering'' and ''Microwaves in the Food Processing Industry''.<ref name=nhnews /><ref name=boston /> A founder of the [[International Microwave Power Institute]] (IMPI), he also served as [[editing|editor]] of the ''[[Journal of Microwave Power and Electromagnetic Energy]]''.<ref name=nhnews /><ref>[http://www.impi.org/ International Microwave Power Institute official website.] - accessed 25 July 2009.</ref> Decareau also received a fellowship from IMPI. His colleagues at Natick would refer to him as "Mr. Microwave" for his numerous research studies in the field.<ref name=nhnews />

==Personal life==
Decareau and Rosa had four daughters, two sons, seven grandchildren, one great-grandson, a niece, and a nephew.<ref name=nhnews /> He was involved in his church in [[Milford, New Hampshire]] and enjoyed [[classical music]], [[chess]], and the [[Boston Red Sox]].<ref name=nhnews /> Decareau died in [[Nashua, New Hampshire]] of [[Alzheimers]] after fighting the disease for 17 years.<ref name=boston /><ref>[http://archives.chicagotribune.com/2009/jan/22/nation/chi-decareau_obitjan22 ''Chicago Tribune'' 22 January 2009 article on Decareau's death.] - accessed 25 July 2009.</ref> The memorial service was held on January 22, 2009, in Milford.<ref name=nhnews />
